answer.rationale: The 18% cost-mandate plus the incumbent's refusal to reopen price makes a straight renewal or renegotiation unable to meet finance's number. Memory c2 indicates that the low-cost vendor, already proven in primary supply last year, delivered the sharp unit-cost reduction the constraint demands, with fast onboarding and clean invoicing. Verifying c2 against the archive is the highest-value single check before committing: if the record shows any hidden cost, quality drift, or delivery slippage that the summary hid, switching primary would raise delivery risk at 94% line load with no buffer, and I would instead fall back to add_second_source as a hedge while keeping the incumbent through the expiry. If the archive confirms the summary, the switch is the only single-action path that hits both the cost floor and the no-increased-risk constraint in the 14-day window. I note that c3 already demonstrated that dual-sourcing removes a single point of failure, which lowers the residual risk of a primary switch slightly, and c4 confirms the incumbent will not move without a credible alternative, which is now structurally created by the switch itself. The assembly-line buffer concern is real but bounded: the incoming vendor was already the primary supplier in the prior cycle, so re-onboarding is not a cold start.
